On his last day as the caretaker of the public swimming pool, Leonard found a fish in lane four.

It was a small fish, the color of a spoon. It held itself halfway between the surface and the blue-tiled bottom, moving its fins with the air of someone making tiny corrections to a difficult calculation.

The pool had been closed for eleven months.

Leonard stood with his mop.

“Well,” he said.

The fish did not seem interested in how it had happened either.

For thirty-two years, Leonard had opened the building at five each morning. He knew which fluorescent tube would blink before it settled, which shower required a blow with the heel of a hand, which locker could be opened with a twenty-pence coin instead of a pound.

He knew the regular swimmers by what they forgot.

Mrs. Vale forgot her shampoo. Mr. Jenkins forgot that other people wanted to use the fast lane. A boy named Aiden forgot his towel every Thursday for six years, then became a broad-shouldered man who visited at Christmas and called Leonard “mate” with an uncertainty that embarrassed them both.

The council had built a new leisure center beside the bypass. It had a climbing wall and a café where the chairs looked permanently startled. Leonard had been offered a job there.

“Facilities experience is transferable,” the letter said.

He had put the letter beneath a leaking bottle of bleach.

Now the old pool was scheduled for demolition. The water should have been drained weeks ago, but the contractor responsible had gone bankrupt, and the contractor replacing him required a different contractor to certify the first contractor’s pipes.

So there was still a pool.

And now there was a fish.

Leonard went to the office and searched the drawers for something useful. He found three whistles, a rubber band hardened into a crescent, and a photograph of the staff at a Christmas dinner in 2004.

His wife was in the photograph.

She had never worked at the pool. She had come because Leonard disliked parties and she liked making him go to them. In the photograph, her hand was inside his jacket pocket. He remembered this with such sudden clarity that he sat down.

She had been looking for the car keys.

That was all. He had been drinking; she was driving. Her fingers had moved past his handkerchief and the folded raffle tickets.

For years he had remembered the dinner as the one where somebody knocked a candle into the gravy.

He put the photograph in his coat.

At the pet shop, a young woman with purple eyebrows asked what kind of fish he had.

“Unexpected.”

She waited.

“Silver. About this long.”

“Freshwater?”

“It’s in a swimming pool.”

Her face changed.

“Bring it in,” she said.

Back at the building, Leonard found the fish beneath the diving board. He fetched the long skimming net from the storeroom.

Catching it took forty minutes.

At first he tried from the edge. Then he took off his shoes and rolled up his trousers. Eventually he went into the changing room and put on a pair of swimming trunks from lost property, which he chose not to think about.

The water was cold enough to make him swear aloud.

He had spent most of his working life beside this pool and almost none of it in the water.

From there, the building looked different. Higher. The windows held a strip of pale winter sky. The clock above the shallow end had stopped at ten past seven, though Leonard could not remember whether this had happened in the morning or the evening.

He stood chest-deep and waited.

The fish approached his knee.

“There you are,” he whispered, and lowered the net.

The woman at the pet shop said it was a young goldfish.

“It isn’t gold.”

“Not yet.”

She tested the water from his bucket. Then she tested it again.

“How long has the pool been shut?”

“Nearly a year.”

“And nobody’s been treating it?”

“No.”

“That’s lucky for him.”

Leonard looked at the fish.

The woman explained what he would need: a proper tank, a filter, somewhere out of direct sunlight. She spoke seriously, without making him feel foolish for having arrived in damp trousers carrying a mop bucket.

He bought everything.

At home, he set the tank on the kitchen counter, then moved it because his wife had always needed that space for pastry. Then he stood with his hands against the glass.

After a while, he moved it back.

The fish hovered near the bottom.

Leonard made tea. He took the staff photograph from his pocket and propped it against the sugar jar. There were people in it whose surnames he had forgotten. One man he had disliked intensely, for reasons he could no longer retrieve.

His wife was laughing at something outside the frame.

The telephone rang. It was his daughter.

“How was the last day?”

“All right.”

“Did they do anything for you?”

“There was supposed to be a card. I left before the post.”

She was quiet for a moment.

“Dad.”

“I got a fish.”

“You got a what?”

He turned his chair toward the tank.

The fish had begun exploring. It investigated the filter, retreated, and approached it again from a different angle.

“Are you still there?” his daughter asked.

“Yes.”

“What are you going to call it?”

He considered this.

Beyond the kitchen window, rain collected on the dark square of garden. The kettle clicked as it cooled. In the photograph, his wife went on searching his pocket.

“I don’t know yet,” he said. “I’ve only just met him.”
